questions.question: A rotating coil in a school a.c. generator is connected across an LED. Explain why the LED flashes on and off as the coil rotates.
questions.answer: The induced e.m.f. alternates in direction; the LED is a diode that conducts in one direction only, so it lights only on alternate half-cycles.
steps: As the coil rotates, the magnetic flux linkage through it changes continuously.
By Faraday's law, an e.m.f. is induced whose size depends on the rate of change of flux linkage.
The flux linkage changes sign over each half turn, so the induced e.m.f. reverses direction (Lenz's law).
The output is therefore an alternating e.m.f., and the current in the circuit reverses each half cycle.
An LED is a diode, which conducts only in its forward direction.
So the LED is lit only during the half-cycles when the current flows forward, giving a flashing effect.

questions.question: Add to the V-t graph of the generator output to show the output when the angular velocity of the coil is halved.
questions.answer: A sine curve of the same shape but with peak 2.5 V and period 0.40 s: it starts at 0, peaks at +2.5 V at 0.10 s, crosses zero at 0.20 s, reaches -2.5 V at 0.30 s and returns to 0 at 0.40 s, completing two cycles by 0.80 s.
steps: The original output is a sine wave of peak 5.0 V and period 0.20 s (four cycles in 0.80 s).
Halving the angular velocity halves the rate of change of flux linkage, so the peak e.m.f. (proportional to omega) halves to 2.5 V.
The period is inversely proportional to omega, so it doubles to 0.40 s, giving only two cycles on the 0.80 s axis.
Draw it starting from zero at t = 0, same phase as the original, with the correct peaks at 0.10 s and 0.30 s.

questions.question: Explain the changes to the V-t graph of the generator output when the angular velocity of the coil is halved.
questions.answer: The peak p.d. halves and the period doubles (frequency halves), so the trace is half as tall and twice as long.
steps: Peak induced e.m.f. = NBA omega, so it is directly proportional to angular velocity omega.
Halving omega therefore halves the peak p.d. (amplitude).
Period T = 2 pi / omega, so halving omega doubles the period.
Frequency is halved because f = 1/T.
On the graph the waveform becomes half as tall and stretched to twice the time length.

questions.question: The mean magnitude of the output p.d. is 3.2 V with B = 0.083 T and coil area 0.0048 m^2 at the original angular velocity. Find the number of turns.
questions.answer: 400 turns (about 4.0 x 10^2)
steps: From the graph the period is T = 0.20 s and the peak p.d. is 5.0 V, so omega = 2 pi / T = 31.4 rad s^-1.
The coil turns from zero flux linkage (plane parallel to the field) to N B A in a quarter period, T/4 = 0.050 s, so the average magnitude of the e.m.f. is N B A / (T/4).
Check with the peak: V_max = N B A omega gives N = 5.0 / (0.083 x 0.0048 x 31.4) = 400, the same (and 3.2 V = (2/pi) x 5.0 V).

questions.question: A proton enters a magnetic field at an angle. Choose the option giving the direction of the force on it as it enters.
questions.answer: C: into the page
steps: The magnetic force on a moving charge, F = q v x B, is perpendicular to both v and B.
The velocity (up and to the right) and the field (to the right) both lie in the plane of the page, so the force must be perpendicular to the page: A and B are wrong.
For a positive proton, with the first finger along B (right) and the second finger along v (up-right), Fleming's left-hand rule gives the thumb (force) pointing into the page, option C.

questions.question: A lever is rotated through 90 degrees by a force that rises steadily from 2.6 N to 9.6 N, applied at right angles to a 4.9 cm lever. Show the work done is about 0.5 J.
questions.answer: W = 0.47 J, which is about 0.5 J as required.
steps: The force increases steadily (linearly), so the average force is (2.6 + 9.6)/2 = 6.1 N.
A rotation of 90 degrees is pi/2 radians.
The force is at right angles to the lever, so the distance moved is the arc length s = r theta = 0.049 x pi/2 = 0.0770 m.
Work done = average force x distance = 6.1 x 0.0770 = 0.47 J.
0.47 J rounds to about 0.5 J, as shown.

questions.question: Explain how an alternating p.d. across the input coil of an iron-cored transformer causes a capacitor to charge through a diode on the output coil.
questions.answer: The alternating input current gives a changing flux in the core, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in the output coil; the diode passes only one half-cycle, so the capacitor charges.
steps: The alternating p.d. drives an alternating current in the input coil.
This alternating current produces a changing magnetic flux in the shared iron core.
The changing flux links the output coil, inducing an alternating e.m.f. in it (mutual induction, Faraday's law).
The diode conducts only in one direction, so only one polarity of the output reaches the capacitor (half-wave rectification).
Charge flows onto the capacitor during each forward half-cycle, and the diode stops it discharging back.
Over many cycles charge builds up, so the capacitor charges to a high p.d. and stores energy.

questions.question: Using the B-t graph for the iron core (1700 turns, area 3.5 x 10^-4 m^2), show the maximum p.d. across the output coil is about 600 V.
questions.answer: epsilon_max = N A (dB/dt)_max = 1700 x 3.5 x 10^-4 x 1.0 x 10^3 = about 6 x 10^2 V
steps: The e.m.f. in the output coil is epsilon = N d(BA)/dt = N A dB/dt, so it is largest where the B-t graph is steepest, at the points where B = 0.

The graph has peak B = 8.3 x 10^-3 T and period 5.0 x 10^-5 s, so the maximum gradient is 2 pi B0 / T = 2 pi x 8.3 x 10^-3 / 5.0 x 10^-5 = 1.0 x 10^3 T s^-1 (a tangent drawn at a zero crossing gives the same).
epsilon_max = 1700 x 3.5 x 10^-4 x 1.0 x 10^3 = 6.0 x 10^2 V, about 600 V, as required.

questions.question: Decide whether the mechanical or the electronic mouse trap stores more energy, using the capacitor charged to 600 V and the discharge graph through 3000 ohm.
questions.answer: The electronic trap stores much more energy: about 270 J, compared with 0.47 J (about 0.5 J) for the mechanical trap.
steps: During discharge V = V0 e^(-t/RC) with V0 = 600 V. The time constant is the time for V to fall to 600/e = 221 V, which the graph gives at t of about 4.5 s.
The mechanical trap needed 0.47 J (average force x distance) to set, so the electronic trap stores far more energy (about 570 times as much).

questions.question: A current-carrying wire lies between magnetic poles with B = 0.070 T. Choose the option giving the force magnitude and direction.
questions.answer: C: 0.070 x 1.5 x 0.050, out of the page (F = 5.3 x 10^-3 N)
steps: The force is F = B I L sin(theta). Only the component of the wire length perpendicular to the field counts: with the field vertical and the wire at an angle, L sin(theta) = the 5.0 cm width of the poles, not the 6.5 cm length along the wire.

The field goes from N (top) to S (bottom), i.e. downwards, and the conventional current flows to the left along the wire. By Fleming's left-hand rule (field down, current left) the force is out of the page, option C.

questions.question: A magnet is dropped through a coil. Choose the table row giving the poles at X (entry) and Y (exit).
questions.answer: B: X is a north pole and Y is a south pole
steps: Entering: the N pole of the magnet approaches the coil end X. By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approach, so end X must become a north pole to repel the incoming north pole.
Leaving: the magnet moves away from the coil, and the induced current opposes this by attracting the magnet back. The end Y nearest the departing north pole must be a south pole to attract it.
X north when entering and Y south when leaving: option B.

questions.question: A model motor coil (10 turns, 5.0 cm by 3.5 cm, 6.9 A, B = 0.07 T) is at 20 degrees to the horizontal. Find the resultant moment about P.
steps: Force on each long side (length 5.0 cm, perpendicular to the horizontal field): F = N B I L = 10 x 0.07 x 6.9 x 0.050 = 0.24 N.
The forces on the two sides are equal and opposite and vertical (a couple). The perpendicular distance between their lines of action is the horizontal separation of X and Y: 0.035 cos 20 = 0.033 m.
Moment = F x d = 0.2415 x 0.035 x cos 20 = 7.9 x 10^-3 N m (equivalently N B I A cos 20 with A = 0.050 x 0.035).

questions.question: A wire makes 10 complete revolutions in 8.3 s. Calculate its angular velocity.
questions.answer: omega = 7.57 rad s-1
steps: One revolution = 2 pi radians, so 10 revolutions = 20 pi = 62.8 rad.
Angular velocity omega = angle / time = 62.8 / 8.3.
omega = 7.57 rad s-1.

questions.question: The wire carries 1.1 A and is at 10 degrees to the vertical, with 3.5 cm of its length in a horizontal field of B = 0.053 T. Find the force on the wire and its direction.
questions.answer: Force = 2.0 x 10^-3 N, directed out of the page (horizontally, perpendicular to both the wire and the field).
steps: The wire is at 10 degrees to the vertical, so it is at 80 degrees to the horizontal field.
F = B I L sin(theta) = 0.053 x 1.1 x 0.035 x sin 80 = 2.0 x 10^-3 N.

The force is perpendicular to both the field (to the right) and the current (downwards along the wire). By Fleming's left-hand rule (field right, current down) the thumb points out of the page, towards the viewer.

questions.question: Explain how steadily increasing the current in the central coil of a tokamak produces a current in the plasma.
questions.answer: The increasing coil current gives a changing flux through the plasma loop, which induces an e.m.f. and so a current in the conducting plasma.
steps: Steadily increasing the current in the central coil increases the magnetic field it produces.
The magnetic flux through the plasma loop, which surrounds the coil, therefore increases steadily.
By Faraday's law, a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in the loop.
The plasma is an electrical conductor, so the e.m.f. drives a current around it.
By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the change in flux, which is why the coil current must keep increasing.

questions.question: The plasma is a cylinder of length 13.2 m and area 2.30 m^2 with resistivity 3.30 x 10^-8 ohm m. Show its resistance is about 1.9 x 10^-7 ohm.
questions.answer: R = 1.9 x 10^-7 ohm (shown).
steps: Resistance of a uniform conductor R = rho L / A.
Numerator = 4.356 x 10^-7 ohm m^2.

questions.question: The current in the central coil rises steadily from zero to its maximum in 25.0 s, giving a flux linkage of 16.9 Wb with the plasma loop. Calculate the heating power in the plasma, using R = 1.9 x 10^-7 ohm.
steps: The flux linkage changes steadily from 0 to 16.9 Wb, so the e.m.f. is constant.
Induced e.m.f. E = change in flux linkage / time = 16.9 / 25.0 = 0.676 V.
Power dissipated in a resistor P = E^2 / R.

questions.question: A current-carrying wire is at an angle to a uniform magnetic field. Choose the graph showing how force F varies as the angle increases from 0 to 90 degrees.
questions.answer: B: a curve starting at zero and rising with decreasing gradient to a maximum at 90 degrees (F proportional to sin theta)
steps: F = B I L sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the wire and the field, so F is proportional to sin(theta).
At theta = 0 the force is zero, and F rises to its maximum value at 90 degrees, with the gradient decreasing as theta approaches 90 degrees (a quarter of a sine curve).
This is graph B (A is convex like theta squared; C and D start at their maximum).

questions.question: A wire between two magnets on a balance changes the reading from 1.500 N to 1.503 N with B = 0.07 T. Choose the current and its direction.
steps: The balance reading rises by 0.003 N, so the magnets are pushed down by 0.003 N and, by Newton's third law, the force on the wire is 0.003 N upwards.
F = B I L, with L = 5 cm = 0.05 m in the field, so I = F / (B L) = 0.003 / (0.07 x 0.05) = 0.043 A.

The field goes from the front N pole to the back S pole (away from the viewer). For an upward force on the wire, Fleming's left-hand rule (field away from viewer, thumb up) gives the current from X to Y (left to right): option A.

questions.question: A magnet falls through a copper tube suspended from a force meter and the meter reading increases. Explain why.
questions.answer: Induced eddy currents in the copper oppose the falling magnet, so the magnet pushes the tube downwards, adding to the reading.
steps: As the magnet falls, the magnetic flux through the copper tube changes.
This induces eddy currents, which are closed loops of current in the copper.
By Lenz's law, the eddy currents oppose the change that produces them.
The eddy currents' magnetic field pushes the magnet upward, opposing its fall.
By Newton's third law, the magnet exerts an equal downward force on the tube.
This extra downward force adds to the tube's weight, so the force meter reading increases.

questions.question: A coil of wire is connected to a resistor. The magnetic flux density through the coil is increased steadily from zero to a maximum value. Which single change would result in a smaller current in the resistor? A increasing the area of the coil in the magnetic field; B increasing the maximum flux density; C increasing the number of turns on the coil; D increasing the time taken to reach the maximum flux density.
questions.answer: D: increasing the time taken to reach the maximum flux density.
steps: Induced e.m.f. E = N A (change in B) / (time), so E is proportional to the rate of change of flux.
The current in the resistor I = E / R, so a smaller rate of change gives a smaller current.
A: increasing the area increases the flux change and so the e.m.f.; C: more turns also increases the e.m.f.
B: a larger maximum B increases the rate of change over the same time, so the current increases.
D: a longer time reduces the rate of change of flux, so the current is smaller.

questions.question: A rectangular coil of N turns is rotated through an angle in a field perpendicular to its plane. Choose the expression for the change in flux linkage.
questions.answer: D: 2N phi
steps: Initially the field is perpendicular to the coil plane and the flux linkage is N phi.
After a rotation of pi radians (180 degrees) the same face is turned to the opposite side, so the field passes through the coil in the opposite direction and the flux linkage is -N phi.
Change = (-N phi) - (N phi) = -2 N phi, so the magnitude of the change is 2 N phi (option D).

questions.question: A proton of speed v enters a field of B = 5.00 T and experiences a force of 1.20 x 10^-11 N. Choose the speed.
steps: The proton moves at right angles to the field, so F = B q v with q = 1.60 x 10^-19 C.
A uses the proton mass instead of its charge, so it is wrong; C and D are the reciprocals.

questions.question: Which statement does not help to explain why electrons can be used to probe nuclei?
questions.answer: B: electrons being part of an atom does not help explain probing nuclei.
steps: Electrons can be accelerated to high energies, giving high momentum and short wavelength (A helps).
Electrons show diffraction, which is needed to probe structure (C helps).
Their wavelength can be similar to nuclear diameters, so they resolve nuclei (D helps).
Being part of an atom says nothing about their ability to probe a nucleus, so B does not help.

questions.question: A carriage of mass 7500 kg starts from rest and a force of 109 kN acts for 2.9 s. Show its velocity is about 40 m s-1.
questions.answer: v = 42 m s-1, which is about 40 m s-1 as required.
steps: Newton's second law: a = F / m = 1.09 x 10^5 / 7500 = 14.5 m s-2.
The carriage starts from rest, so u = 0.
This rounds to about 40 m s-1, as shown.

questions.question: Assuming no resistive forces, deduce whether the carriage (leaving at about 40 m s-1) reaches the top of an 81 m tower.
questions.answer: Yes: the maximum height is about 90 m, which is greater than 81 m.
steps: With no resistive forces, the kinetic energy at the base converts fully to gravitational potential energy.
Using v = 42.1 m s-1: mgh = (1/2) m v^2, so h = v^2 / (2g).
90 m is greater than the 81 m tower height, so the carriage reaches the top (with about 9 m to spare).

questions.question: Explain why an aluminium fin leaves the gap between magnets at a much slower speed than it entered.
questions.answer: Eddy currents in the moving aluminium oppose its motion (Lenz's law) and the kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy.
steps: As the fin moves through the magnetic field, the flux through it changes.
This induces eddy currents in the aluminium fin.
The eddy currents are in a magnetic field, so they experience a force (F = BIL).
By Lenz's law this force opposes the motion of the fin, so it decelerates.
Work done against this force transfers kinetic energy into thermal energy (I^2 R heating) in the aluminium.
So the fin loses kinetic energy and leaves the gap much more slowly.

questions.question: Coil 1 carries the alternating current shown for two cycles. Choose the graph of the induced e.m.f. across coil 2.
questions.answer: B: a cosine-shaped curve starting at its minimum, the negative of the gradient of the I-t sine curve
steps: The e.m.f. induced in coil 2 is proportional to minus the rate of change of the flux, which is proportional to -dI/dt.

I is a sine wave starting at zero, so dI/dt is a cosine wave (maximum at t = 0), and the e.m.f. is a negative cosine: it starts at its minimum, passes through zero at a quarter cycle and reaches its maximum at half a cycle, two cycles in all.
A is a negative sine (starts at zero) and C and D are rectified, so only B has the correct shape and phase.

questions.question: A wire of length l carrying current I lies in the plane of a magnetic field B. Choose the table row giving the force.
questions.answer: A: B I l cos(phi), into the page
steps: phi is the angle between the field and the normal to the wire, so the angle between the wire and the field is 90 - phi.
The force magnitude is B I l sin(90 - phi) = B I l cos(phi), which leaves A or B.
The field is to the right and the current is up and to the right in the plane of the page. By Fleming's left-hand rule (field right, current up-right) the force is into the page, so the answer is A.

questions.question: The aluminium plate of length 15.0 cm takes 0.19 s to pass light gate 1. The vehicle has mass 0.40 kg. Show its momentum is about 0.3 N s.
questions.answer: p = 0.32 N s, which is about 0.3 N s as shown.
steps: Speed of the vehicle = distance / time = 0.150 m / 0.19 s = 0.789 m s-1.
Momentum p = m v = 0.40 x 0.789 kg m s-1.
p = 0.316 N s, which rounds to about 0.3 N s, as shown.

questions.question: The kinetic energy falls by 10% between the magnet and light gate 2. Calculate the velocity at light gate 2 (initial speed 0.789 m s-1, mass 0.40 kg).
steps: Initial kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 = 0.5 x 0.40 x (0.789)^2 = 0.125 J.
After a 10% reduction the kinetic energy is 0.9 x 0.125 = 0.112 J.
v = 0.75 m s-1 at light gate 2.

questions.question: Explain why a current was produced in the aluminium plate as it passed between the poles of the magnet.
questions.answer: The plate moves through a magnetic field, so the flux through it changes and induces an e.m.f. that drives eddy currents in the conductor.
steps: The aluminium plate is a conductor moving through a magnetic field.
Its motion changes the magnetic flux through the plate as it enters and leaves the field.
By electromagnetic induction (Faraday's law), an e.m.f. is induced in the plate.
This e.m.f. drives closed loops of current (eddy currents) within the aluminium.

questions.question: Explain why the kinetic energy of the vehicle decreases as the aluminium plate moves between the magnet poles.
questions.answer: The eddy currents experience a force that opposes motion (Lenz's law); work done against it is transferred to thermal energy in the plate.
steps: The eddy currents in the plate are in the magnetic field, so they experience a magnetic force.
By Lenz's law this force opposes the motion of the plate.
Work is done against this opposing force as the plate moves.
The work done is transferred to thermal energy in the aluminium, so the kinetic energy of the vehicle falls.

questions.question: Using the table of plate thickness and percentage kinetic energy reduction, show the reduction is proportional to thickness.
questions.answer: Percentage reduction / thickness is constant (20 % per mm) for all three plates, so the reduction is proportional to thickness.
steps: Calculate reduction / thickness: initial plate 10 / 0.50 = 20; second plate 16 / 0.80 = 20; third plate 22 / 1.1 = 20.
The ratio is the same (20 % per mm) for every plate, so the percentage reduction in kinetic energy is directly proportional to the thickness (the line through the origin).

questions.question: Suggest why the percentage reduction in kinetic energy increases as the thickness of the aluminium plate increases.
questions.answer: A thicker plate has a larger cross-section and lower resistance, so larger eddy currents and a bigger braking force, removing more kinetic energy.
steps: Resistance of the plate R = rho L / A, and a thicker plate has a larger cross-sectional area A.
So a thicker plate has lower resistance.
The induced e.m.f. is the same, so the eddy current I = e.m.f./R is larger.
A larger eddy current gives a larger magnetic braking force (F = BIL), so more energy is transferred to thermal energy.
A larger fraction of the kinetic energy is therefore lost.

questions.question: State the name of the term and its unit in the form of Faraday's law shown in the question.
questions.answer: N phi is the magnetic flux linkage; its unit is the weber (Wb, equal to T m^2).
steps: N is the number of turns and phi the magnetic flux through each turn, so N phi is the magnetic flux linkage of the coil.
The unit is the weber (Wb), which is the same as tesla metre squared (T m^2), since N is a pure number.

questions.question: A 500-turn coil of radius 3.0 mm lies between electromagnet poles, with B varying with time as a graph. Determine the maximum e.m.f.
questions.answer: Maximum e.m.f. = 1.3 V
steps: Area of the coil A = pi r^2 = pi x (3.0 x 10^-3)^2 = 2.8 x 10^-5 m^2.
The e.m.f. is epsilon = N A dB/dt, a maximum where the B-t graph is steepest, at B = 0.
The graph has peak B = 0.30 T and period 0.020 s, so the maximum gradient is 2 pi B0 / T = 2 pi x 0.30 / 0.020 = 94 T s^-1 (consistent with a tangent at a zero crossing).
epsilon_max = 500 x 2.8 x 10^-5 x 94 = 1.3 V.

questions.question: A student suggests an aluminium disc will start to rotate as a magnet is moved around it, in the same direction as the magnet. Discuss this suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is valid: the changing flux induces eddy currents, and by Lenz's law the disc is dragged in the same direction as the magnet moves relative to it.
steps: Moving the magnet around the disc changes the magnetic flux through the disc, so eddy currents are induced in it.
The disc is a conductor, so the induced currents flow in closed loops in the disc.
The eddy currents lie in the magnet's field, so they experience a force (F = BIL).
By Lenz's law the force opposes the relative motion between magnet and disc, so the disc is pushed along with the magnet.
The disc therefore starts to rotate, in the same direction as the magnet is moved.
The disc never quite reaches the speed of the magnet, because a relative motion is needed to induce the currents.

questions.question: Two balloons of mass 1.1 g each, with equal negative charges, repel in diagram 2. Show the repulsive force is about 1 x 10^-3 N.
steps: The threads are fixed 0.21 m apart (as in diagram 1) and the balloon centres are 0.47 m apart in diagram 2, so each balloon is displaced sideways by (0.47 - 0.21) / 2 = 0.13 m from the vertical below its support.
The thread length is 1.22 m, so tan(theta) = 0.13 / sqrt(1.22^2 - 0.13^2) = 0.13 / 1.213 = 0.107.
In equilibrium T cos(theta) = mg and T sin(theta) = F, so F = mg tan(theta).

questions.question: Using the repulsive force of about 1 x 10^-3 N, show each balloon carries a charge of about 2 x 10^-7 C.
steps: The balloon charges act as point charges at the centres, 0.47 m apart: F = kQ^2 / r^2.
Q = 1.7 x 10^-7 C, which is about 2 x 10^-7 C.

questions.question: One balloon is removed. The remaining balloon has charge of about -2 x 10^-7 C. Calculate the electric potential at 0.30 m from its centre.
questions.answer: V = -6.0 x 10^3 V (about -6.0 kV)
steps: The charge acts as if concentrated at the balloon centre, so the potential is V = kQ / r.
Charge Q = -2.0 x 10^-7 C (negative, as the balloons were given negative charge).

questions.question: A strong magnet falls through two copper tubes of equal length and area; tube B has a vertical slit. Discuss the difference in fall times.
questions.answer: The magnet falls more slowly through solid tube A, because eddy currents can circulate around it; the slit in tube B blocks the loops, so B has smaller eddy currents and the magnet falls faster.
steps: Falling magnet changes the flux through the copper; eddy currents are induced in the tube (Faraday's law).
In tube A the eddy currents can circulate completely around the tube, so they are large.
By Lenz's law the large eddy currents produce a large upward force, which slows the magnet.
The vertical slit in tube B interrupts the circulating path, so the eddy currents are much smaller.
The braking force is therefore smaller in B, so the magnet falls faster and takes less time through tube B.
Tube A gives the longer fall time.

questions.question: Which of the following gives the base units of the tesla?
questions.answer: C: kg A-1 s-2
steps: Magnetic flux density B = F / (I L), so units are N / (A m).
A newton is kg m s-2, so N / (A m) = kg m s-2 / (A m).
Simplify: kg m s-2 / (A m) = kg A-1 s-2 (the metres cancel).

questions.question: Two coils L and M are placed together. Which of the following could produce an alternating e.m.f. across coil M?
questions.answer: A: an alternating current in coil L.
steps: An e.m.f. is induced only when the flux linked with coil M is changing.
A constant current in L gives constant flux, so B produces no induced e.m.f.
A decreasing or increasing current gives a changing flux, but only a steady change in one direction, not alternating.
An alternating current in L gives an alternating changing flux, which induces an alternating e.m.f. in M.

questions.question: A square coil PQRS of side l carries a clockwise current I, with its plane parallel to a field of flux density B. Choose the table row that is correct.
questions.answer: A: side PQ has zero magnetic force
steps: The force on a current-carrying side is F = B I l sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the side and the field, which is zero when they are parallel.
The field is to the right, parallel to sides PQ and RS (current to the right along PQ and to the left along RS), so these have no force: A is correct and C is wrong.
Sides QR and SP are perpendicular to the field and have force B I l; by Fleming's left-hand rule SP (current upwards) is into the page, and QR is out of the page, so B and D are wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following is a possible unit for magnetic flux?
questions.answer: A: T m2 (equal to the weber, Wb)
steps: Magnetic flux Phi = B A, where B is in tesla and A is in m^2.
So the unit of flux is T m^2, which is the weber (1 Wb = 1 T m^2).
B, C and D have the wrong powers of m or use the weber incorrectly, so A is the only valid unit.

questions.question: A student quickly moves part of a closed wire loop downwards between two magnets on a balance. Explain how the balance reading changed.
questions.answer: The reading increases: the moving wire cuts the field, inducing a current whose force on the wire opposes the motion; the reaction pushes the magnets down onto the balance.
steps: Moving the wire downwards between the magnets cuts the magnetic field lines, changing the flux through the closed loop.
This induces an e.m.f. and a current in the loop.
The current in the wire lying in the magnetic field experiences a force (F = BIL).
By Lenz's law, this force on the wire opposes its downward motion, so it acts upwards.
By Newton's third law, the wire pushes the magnets downwards with an equal force.
The balance reading therefore increases while the wire is moving.

questions.question: A wire moves vertically downwards between two magnets (magnet length 34 mm, height 20 mm, B = 0.35 T) at 2.2 m s-1. Calculate the maximum p.d. across the wire.
steps: The wire is horizontal across the faces of the magnets, so the length of wire in the field is the magnet length, L = 34 mm = 0.034 m (the 20 mm height is not needed).
The maximum p.d. occurs while the whole length is moving through the uniform field at constant speed: epsilon = B L v.

questions.question: A search coil is rotated from parallel to perpendicular to a magnetic field, and a p.d. is detected. Explain why.
questions.answer: Rotating the coil changes the flux linkage through it, which induces an e.m.f. across its terminals.
steps: The flux linkage through the coil depends on its orientation to the field.
As the coil rotates, the flux linkage changes.
By Faraday's law, a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in the coil.
This e.m.f. appears as the p.d. across the terminals.

questions.question: A coil of diameter 25 mm lies with its axis parallel to a field of flux density 0.18 T. Show the initial flux is about 9 x 10^-5 Wb.
questions.answer: Phi = 8.8 x 10^-5 Wb, which is about 9 x 10^-5 Wb as shown.
steps: Radius r = 25 mm / 2 = 12.5 mm = 0.0125 m.
The axis is parallel to the field, so the coil plane is perpendicular to B and the full area is used.

questions.question: Using the flux-time graph of the search coil (5000 turns) during rotation, determine the maximum p.d. across the terminals.
questions.answer: 2.3 V (about 2.3 to 2.4 V)
steps: epsilon = N d(phi)/dt, so the maximum p.d. is where the flux-time graph is steepest, at the end of the rotation (t = 0.30 s), where the flux falls to zero.

The gradient there is about 4.6 x 10^-4 Wb s^-1 (for example, the flux falls from 1.85 x 10^-5 Wb at 0.26 s to 0 at 0.30 s). This also equals phi0 x omega = 8.8 x 10^-5 x (pi / 0.60) = 4.6 x 10^-4 Wb s^-1.
epsilon_max = 5000 x 4.6 x 10^-4 = 2.3 V.

questions.question: The coil terminals are shorted and the coil is rotated clockwise. A student says the current at side X is into the page. Comment on the statement.
questions.answer: The student is correct: the current at X is into the page.
steps: As the coil rotates clockwise, side X (at the top) moves to the right, at right angles to the downward magnetic field, so it cuts the field lines and an e.m.f. is induced in it.
Fleming's right-hand rule (thumb = motion to the right, first finger = field downwards) gives the induced current (second finger) into the page at X.
Check with Lenz's law: a current into the page at X in a downward field gives a force to the left on X, which opposes its motion to the right. So the statement is correct.

questions.question: A current-carrying wire lies between magnetic poles with B = 0.85 T. Choose the option giving the force in newtons and its direction.
questions.answer: A: 0.85 x 0.17 x 0.052 into the page (F = 7.5 x 10^-3 N); the 0.085 printed in the options is presumably a misprint for the 0.85 T given in the question.
steps: The field goes from N (top) to S (bottom), downwards. The part of the wire length that is perpendicular to the field is its horizontal extent, the 5.2 cm width of the poles, so F = B I (0.052) with no sin 35 factor (the wire length in the field is 0.052 / cos 35 and its angle to the field is 55 degrees, so L sin 55 = 0.052).
Direction: the current flows to the right and down along the wire with the field downwards; by Fleming's left-hand rule the force is into the page, so option A.

questions.question: A bar magnet is dropped through a small coil connected to a data logger. Explain the variation of e.m.f. with time shown in the output graph.
questions.answer: A positive peak as the magnet enters, zero when it is in the middle of the coil, then a larger, narrower negative peak as it leaves, because the flux linkage first increases then decreases and the magnet is speeding up.
steps: By Faraday's law the e.m.f. is the rate of change of flux linkage. As the magnet's north pole approaches and enters the coil the flux linkage increases, so an e.m.f. is induced and it rises to a peak.
When the middle of the magnet is at the coil the flux linkage is at its maximum, so its rate of change (and the e.m.f.) is zero: the graph crosses zero.
As the magnet leaves, the flux linkage decreases, so by Lenz's law the e.m.f. reverses direction, giving a negative peak.

The magnet is accelerating under gravity, so it is moving faster when it leaves than when it entered; the flux changes more quickly, so the second peak is taller and narrower. The areas of the two peaks are equal in size, since the total change in flux linkage is the same.
Before and after the passage of the magnet the flux linkage is constant (almost zero) so the e.m.f. is zero.

questions.question: A copper rod moves at 3.5 x 10^-2 m s-1 along rails 7.5 cm apart in a uniform field of B = 150 mT. Calculate the induced e.m.f.
steps: The rod moves perpendicular to the field and has length d between the rails.
Motional e.m.f. E = B d v (Faraday's law applied to a moving conductor).

questions.question: Explain the direction of the induced e.m.f. across the copper rod PQ.
questions.answer: The induced e.m.f. acts from P to Q (Q is the positive end), because the force on the induced current must oppose the rod's motion (Lenz's law).
steps: The rod moves to the left with velocity v in a field B directed downwards (into the page in the view from above).
Using Fleming's right-hand rule (thumb = motion to the left, first finger = field into the page), the induced current in the rod, the second finger, points from P to Q (down the page).

Check with Lenz's law: with current from P to Q, the force on the rod is I L x B, which points to the right, opposing the leftward motion. This is the direction needed to oppose the change that produces the e.m.f., so the e.m.f. acts from P to Q.

questions.question: A metal rod in a field of B = 120 mT carries 3.6 A. The balance reading increases by 2.8 g when the switch is closed. Calculate the length L of rod in the field.
steps: The balance reading increase equals the force on the rod (reaction on magnets): F = 2.8 x 10^-3 kg x 9.81 = 0.0275 N.
Force on a current-carrying conductor perpendicular to the field: F = B I L.

questions.question: An aeroplane flies at speed v across the vertical component of Earth's magnetic field, with 35 m between its wingtips. An e.m.f. of 0.40 V is induced. Deduce whether this supports the pilot's 250 m s-1 speed.
questions.answer: No: 0.40 V implies about 280 m s-1; a speed of 250 m s-1 would give about 0.36 V.
steps: Motional e.m.f. across the wings E = B_v L v, with L = 35 m and B_v = 41 uT (text shows 41 T; the micro symbol has been lost).
Rearranging for the 0.40 V value: v = E / (B_v L) = 0.40 / (41 x 10^-6 x 35) = 280 m s-1.
The measured 0.40 V is about 10% above the value for 250 m s-1, so it does not support the pilot's statement.

questions.question: Explain why an iron kettle heats up when an alternating current flows through a coil wound on a soft iron core beneath it.
questions.answer: The alternating current gives a changing flux that induces eddy currents in the iron kettle; the resistance of the iron converts their energy to thermal energy.
steps: The alternating current in the coil produces a changing magnetic field in the soft iron core.
The changing flux passes through the kettle base, which is a conductor.
By Faraday's law, an e.m.f. is induced in the kettle, driving eddy currents in it.
The kettle has electrical resistance, so the eddy currents dissipate energy as heat (I^2 R).
Lenz's law: the eddy currents oppose the changing flux, but they still flow and produce heating.
The heat generated in the kettle base raises the water temperature.

questions.question: The cooker surface is not a conductor. Explain why the egg cooks only where it is in contact with the steel pan.
questions.answer: Eddy currents heat the steel pan itself, and heat reaches the egg only by conduction where the egg touches the pan.
steps: The cooker surface is not a conductor, so no eddy currents or heating occur in it.
The changing field induces eddy currents in the steel pan, which heats the pan through its resistance.
Heat is transferred to the egg by conduction only where it is in direct contact with the hot pan.

questions.question: A proton of speed v enters a uniform field of 45 mT and experiences a force of 1.35 x 10^-13 N. Choose the expression for v.
steps: The proton moves at right angles to the field, so F = B q v and v = F / (B q).
A does not convert mT to T and B and D use the proton mass, which does not appear in F = Bqv.

questions.question: A magnet is moved away from a coil, producing a current. Choose the table row giving the poles at X and Y.
questions.answer: B: X is a north pole and Y is a south pole
steps: The south pole of the magnet is nearest the coil end X, and the magnet is being moved away, so the flux through the coil decreases.
By Lenz's law the induced current opposes this by attracting the magnet back: the coil end X nearest the magnet must be a north pole (attracting the south pole of the magnet).
The other end, Y, is then a south pole, so the row is X north, Y south: B.

questions.question: A wire between bar magnets has force 4.8 x 10^-4 N with B = 0.024 T and length 0.010 m. Choose the current.
steps: F = B I L for a wire perpendicular to the field, so I = F / (B L).
A multiplies the quantities, B and D put B or L the wrong way up.

questions.question: A current-carrying wire lies between two bar magnets with current into the page. Choose the diagram showing the force direction.
questions.answer: A: the force is downwards (down the page)
steps: The wire sits between the N pole of the left magnet and the S pole of the right magnet, so the field points from left to right.
The current is into the page. By Fleming's left-hand rule (first finger to the right, second finger into the page) the thumb (force) points down the page.
This is diagram A (arrow pointing down).

questions.question: An electron moves horizontally through a field at 24 degrees to the vertical, with force into the page. Choose the row giving the magnitude and direction of v.
questions.answer: D: v = F / (B x e x sin 66), directed from Y to X
steps: The velocity is horizontal along XY and the field is 24 degrees from the vertical, so the angle between v and B is 90 - 24 = 66 degrees.
F = B e v sin(66), so v = F / (B e sin 66): C or D.

The force on the electron is into the page. For a negative charge the force is opposite to that on a positive charge, so a velocity from X to Y would give a force out of the page and a velocity from Y to X gives a force into the page.
So the direction is from Y to X: option D.

questions.question: Explain why the coil of the model motor rotates clockwise, viewed from the end, with current in direction ABDC.
questions.answer: The two sides AC and BD carry current in opposite directions in the field from N to S, so they feel forces in opposite directions (up on one side, down on the other), which form a couple turning the coil clockwise.
steps: The field points from the N pole to the S pole (to the left, horizontal). The sides AC and BD are perpendicular to the field and carry currents in opposite directions (C to A and B to D).
Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the force on BD (near the N pole) is downwards and the force on AC (near the S pole) is upwards. The sides AB and DC are parallel to the field and feel no force.
The equal and opposite forces on opposite sides of the axle form a couple, which gives a clockwise moment about the axle when viewed from the end.

questions.question: Calculate the resultant moment about the axle of the magnetic forces on the coil (32 turns, 5.0 cm x 3.5 cm, 0.24 A, B = 0.68 T).
steps: In the position shown the coil plane is parallel to the field, so the moment of the couple is a maximum.
Force on each long side: F = N B I L = 32 x 0.68 x 0.24 x 0.050 = 0.26 N.
The two forces are equal and opposite, a perpendicular distance equal to the coil width apart, so moment = F x d = 0.26 x 0.035.
Moment = 9.1 x 10^-3 N m (equals N B I A with A = 0.050 x 0.035).

questions.question: The student pushes one side of the coil down so it rotates. Explain why a reading may appear on the sensitive voltmeter.
questions.answer: Rotating the coil changes the flux linkage through it, which induces an e.m.f. that gives a reading on the connected voltmeter.
steps: Rotating the coil in the magnetic field changes the flux linkage through the coil.
By Faraday's law, a changing flux linkage induces an e.m.f. in the coil.
The coil is connected to the voltmeter, forming a complete circuit.
So the induced e.m.f. (and current) gives a reading on the voltmeter.

questions.question: Deduce whether a quarter turn of the coil (from horizontal to vertical, 0.080 s) produces a reading on a voltmeter that reads 0.1 V.
questions.answer: Yes: the average e.m.f. is about 0.48 V, which is larger than the 0.1 V resolution, so a reading will be shown.
steps: In the horizontal position the coil plane is parallel to the horizontal field, so the flux linkage is zero; in the vertical position the plane is perpendicular to the field, so the flux linkage is N B A.
Average e.m.f. = change in flux linkage / time = 0.038 / 0.080 = 0.48 V.
This is much more than the 0.1 V resolution of the voltmeter, so a reading would be shown (and the peak e.m.f. is larger still).

questions.question: Explain how a large p.d. is produced across the secondary coil of a spark plug circuit when the switch is opened.
questions.answer: Opening the switch makes the primary current fall to zero very quickly, so the flux changes rapidly and a large e.m.f. is induced in the secondary coil.
steps: The primary current falls to zero almost immediately when the switch is opened.
The magnetic flux in the iron core falls to zero very quickly.
The secondary coil has many turns, and the rate of change of flux linkage is very large.
By Faraday's law, the induced e.m.f. is N dPhi/dt, which is very large because dt is very small.
This large p.d. across the secondary creates the strong electric field across the spark gap.

questions.question: The gap is 0.75 mm. The secondary has 30 000 turns of diameter 16 mm, B falls from a maximum of 0.34 T to zero in 2.0 x 10^-5 s. Calculate the electric field strength in the gap, assuming it is uniform.
steps: Area of one turn A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi (0.008)^2 = 2.01 x 10^-4 m^2.
Change in flux per turn = B A = 0.34 x 2.01 x 10^-4 = 6.84 x 10^-5 Wb.
Induced p.d. V = N (change in flux) / time = 30 000 x 6.84 x 10^-5 / (2.0 x 10^-5) = 1.03 x 10^5 V.

questions.question: Using Lenz's law, explain why the current in the primary coil does not reach its maximum value instantaneously when the switch is closed.
questions.answer: As the current rises, the changing flux induces a back e.m.f. that opposes the increase, so the current grows gradually.
steps: When the switch closes, the current increases and so does the flux in the coil core.
The changing flux induces an e.m.f. in the same coil (self-induction).
By Lenz's law, this induced e.m.f. opposes the change that causes it (a back e.m.f.).
The back e.m.f. reduces the net p.d. driving the current, so the current rises gradually to its maximum.

questions.question: A 90 m power cable carries 700 A. Near the pylons the Earth's field is 48 uT at 20 degrees to the vertical. Determine the force on the cable.
steps: The cable is horizontal and the field is at 20 degrees to the vertical, so the angle between the current and the field is 90 - 20 = 70 degrees.
F = B I L sin(theta) = 48 x 10^-6 x 700 x 90 x sin 70.
F = 3.02 x 0.940 = 2.8 N, at right angles to both the cable and the field.

questions.question: A key card with bar magnets is pulled through a card reader with a coil and voltage sensor. Explain how the sensor detects the orientation of the magnetic poles.
questions.answer: Each magnet's field produces a change in flux through the coil as it passes; the polarity of the induced voltage depends on the pole orientation.
steps: As the card moves through the reader, each magnet's field passes through the coil and changes the flux linkage.
By Faraday's law, each change induces a voltage across the coil.
Reversing a magnet's pole reverses the direction of its field, so the flux change has the opposite sign.
The sensor therefore sees a voltage of positive or negative polarity for each magnet, showing its pole orientation.

questions.question: The card moves 9.0 cm in 0.032 s. Using 25 turns, B = 2.4 x 10^-5 T and magnet width 0.98 mm, deduce whether the induced voltage exceeds 1.5 x 10^-6 V.
questions.answer: Yes: the induced e.m.f. is about 1.7 x 10^-6 V, which is greater than 1.5 x 10^-6 V.
steps: Speed of card v = 0.090 m / 0.032 s = 2.81 m s-1.
Use E = N B w v, where w is the magnet width (0.98 x 10^-3 m).
Since 1.65 x 10^-6 V > 1.5 x 10^-6 V, the card reader can determine the pole orientation.

questions.question: Two coils P and Q are close together with an alternating supply across P. Choose the row giving the largest e.m.f. in Q by its turns and separation.
questions.answer: C: more turns in coil Q, closer together
steps: The e.m.f. in Q is N_Q times the rate of change of the flux through each turn of Q, so more turns in coil Q give a larger e.m.f.
Bringing Q closer to P means more of the changing flux from P links with Q (less flux leakage), so the e.m.f. is larger.
Both effects together give the largest e.m.f.: more turns and closer together (option C).

questions.question: A proton experiences a force of 6.5 x 10^-13 N in a field of B = 0.52 T. Calculate its speed.
questions.answer: v = 7.8 x 10^6 m s-1 (assuming the proton enters perpendicular to the field)
steps: Magnetic force on a charge F = B q v for velocity perpendicular to the field.
Rearrange: v = F / (B q).

questions.question: Draw on the diagram the path of the proton in the magnetic field.
questions.answer: A circular arc starting at the proton and curving downwards (clockwise), always at right angles to its velocity, of constant radius.
steps: The force on the positive proton is F = q v x B. With v to the right and B out of the page the force is downwards, at right angles to v.
The force stays perpendicular to the velocity, so the speed is constant and the path is a circular arc, with its centre below the point of entry; it curves downwards and turns clockwise.

questions.question: Explain how a mobile phone charges when placed near a wireless charger that has an alternating current in a coil.
questions.answer: The alternating current in the charger coil produces a changing flux that links the phone's coil, inducing an alternating e.m.f. which is rectified to charge the battery.
steps: The alternating current in the charger's coil produces a changing magnetic flux.
Some of this flux links the coil in the phone (mutual induction).
By Faraday's law, the changing flux induces an alternating e.m.f. in the phone's coil.
The phone's circuit rectifies this alternating e.m.f. to a direct p.d., which charges the battery.

questions.question: The coil on the a.c. supply has 50 turns of diameter 4.0 cm, with a maximum B of 18 mT. Calculate its maximum flux linkage.
questions.answer: Flux linkage = 1.1 x 10^-3 Wb
steps: Radius r = 4.0 cm / 2 = 0.020 m, so area A = pi r^2 = 1.26 x 10^-3 m^2.
Flux per turn at maximum = B A = 0.018 x 1.26 x 10^-3 = 2.26 x 10^-5 Wb.
Flux linkage = N B A = 50 x 2.26 x 10^-5 = 1.13 x 10^-3 Wb.
The maximum flux linkage is 1.1 x 10^-3 Wb.

questions.question: Suggest why the maximum p.d. across the voltmeter coil is less than the maximum p.d. of the a.c. supply.
questions.answer: Not all the flux from the supply coil links the second coil (flux leakage), so the induced p.d. is smaller.
steps: The two coils are not perfectly coupled, so some flux from the supply coil does not pass through the second coil.
Since the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the flux linked, the induced p.d. is smaller than the supply p.d.

questions.question: A wire of length 40 mm carries 3.1 A in a field between magnets, and the balance reading increases by 0.45 g. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
steps: Force on the wire equals the balance increase: F = 4.5 x 10^-4 kg x 9.81 = 4.41 x 10^-3 N.
Force on a conductor perpendicular to the field: F = B I L.
